findings.title: The model-ID prefix is the only residency control on Bedrock, and AWS's own sample code uses the global one
findings.claim: For Claude Sonnet 5 on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, In-Region inference is not-supported in every AWS region including ap-southeast-2 (Sydney); the only choices are the us./eu./au. geo profiles or global. AWS documents `au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` as keeping data within Australia regions and `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` as routing worldwide with no residency constraints, so a one-token string difference is the whole difference between an AU-resident product and an offshore one, invisible to the type system and to the AWS SDK. Two corrections to the wave 1 form. The Sydney-to-Melbourne destination pair is an inference, not documentation: AWS publishes only "Australia regions" for this model, though the model card's own table shows ap-southeast-2 and ap-southeast-4 as the only two APAC regions with Geo supported, which is where the inference comes from. And the abuse-detection warning does not raise the stakes here: Bedrock is zero-data-retention by default and stores nothing for Sonnet 5, so the exposure is routing alone. A genuinely single-region deployment needs the bedrock-mantle endpoint (In-Region supported only in us-east-1, us-gov-west-1, eu-north-1, eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-4 Melbourne), where Converse, Invoke, Guardrails, Knowledge base, Model evaluation, Prompt management, Flows and Agents are all unsupported.
findings.evidence: AWS Bedrock model card for Claude Sonnet 5, re-fetched by the reconciler 2026-09-05: bedrock-runtime In-Region column reads not-supported for all 30+ listed regions including ap-southeast-2; Geo is supported in APAC only at ap-southeast-2 and ap-southeast-4; data-residency bullets read verbatim "AU geo (au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): Keeps data within Australia regions" and "Global (global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): Routes worldwide with no residency constraints"; bedrock-mantle In-Region supported in exactly five regions with Converse and Invoke both not-supported. The page's own Messages API sample code reads model="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5" — the copy-paste default is the non-resident one. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-anthropic-claude-sonnet-5.html . Verifier correction: the Sydney/Melbourne pair came from the 2025-10-31 Sonnet 4.5/Haiku 4.5 blog, not this model, and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/abuse-detection.html states Bedrock "uses a zero data retention (ZDR) data security model" and "by default, Amazon Bedrock does not store model inputs or outputs", with retention listed only for named models, which do not include Sonnet 5.
findings.action: Ask the work team to grep the repo for `global.anthropic` and `apac.anthropic` on Monday. Then make the prefix un-fumbleable: one Effect Layer that builds the model ID from a Residency tag, an IAM/SCP deny on non-AU destination regions, and a CI check failing any literal model ID that does not start `au.`. Pin the model family in the same check, not just the geo prefix, because retention policy is per-model. Do not rely on a review convention.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q4 tools

findings.title: The TGA moved from review to compliance action against AI scribes in August 2026, and the deployer is a target
findings.claim: As of August 2026 the TGA has moved from review into active compliance action against organisations that deployed scribes operating as unapproved medical devices, citing scope creep, AI influencing clinician decisions, weak transparency and absent post-market monitoring. Its February 2026 guidance names "feature creep" — a scribe that starts suggesting diagnoses or recommending treatment pathways — as adding a new intended use and creating a different kind of medical device. Whether clinician sign-off keeps a documentation-only scribe out of scope must be read off the TGA's own digital-scribes page rather than inferred; the cited law-firm piece does not say it. The enforcement risk sits with the deploying organisation as well as the vendor, and absent post-market monitoring is a named deficiency. RACGP published its first formal AI-scribe guidance in October 2025 (consent, clinician responsibility, data privacy) and its newsGP poll put GP use at 40% in November 2025, up from 22% in August 2024.
findings.evidence: Medical Republic, 2026-08-04, quoting the TGA product quality division head at HIC2026: "When it comes to digital scribes, this review has moved into compliance action", targeting "organisations who have deployed a scribe that's operated as a medical device and have not sought medical device regulatory approval", over "scope creep, inclusion of AI that's influencing decisions of clinicians, and a general lack of transparency" — https://www.medicalrepublic.com.au/tga-flags-compliance-action-on-ai-scribes-as-review-finds-safety-concerns/127888 . Clayton Utz insight, 24 July 2026, carries the feature-creep quote but, asked directly, "does not state that scribes are excluded from medical device regulation when a clinician reviews and approves outputs" — https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2026/july/healthcare-software-tga-clarifies-when-ai-will-be-regulated-as-a-medical-device . Adoption figures: https://www.medicalrepublic.com.au/how-many-gps-are-actually-using-ai-scribes/125763 . Primary source still to be read: https://www.tga.gov.au/products/medical-devices/software-and-artificial-intelligence-ai/overview/types-software-based-medical-devices/digital-scribes (timed out for the verifier at 60s).
findings.action: Read the TGA digital-scribes page directly before quoting any scope rule to the team; the law-firm summary does not carry the sign-off conditional. Add one line to definition of ready: "does this feature produce a recommendation a clinician could act on without independent judgement?" If yes it is a regulatory decision before it is an estimate. Make the sign-off event an audited domain object, and treat post-market monitoring as a compliance artefact, not a nice-to-have — which is what makes the in-note rating widget below load-bearing.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: A dated AU privacy deadline lands 10 December 2026
findings.claim: The Privacy Act's automated decision-making transparency obligation commences 10 December 2026. From that date, APP entities that use personal information in ADM with the potential to affect an individual's rights or interests must disclose in their privacy policy what information is used, what kinds of decisions are made, and how a person can seek meaningful human review. This is confirmed on the OAIC's own consultation page, so the earlier medium confidence was understated. Two attached propositions are not supported by that page and still need a primary source before they are put in front of the team: that health service providers are in scope irrespective of the $3m turnover threshold, and that OAIC guidance is due September 2026 (the page says the consultation closed 15 June 2026).
findings.evidence: OAIC, Consultation on Guidance for Transparency in Automated Decision Making, page dated 18 May 2026: "From 10 December 2026, APP entities that use personal information in ADM with the potential to affect rights or interests will be required to provide information in their privacy policies." https://www.oaic.gov.au/engage-with-us/consultations/consultation-on-guidance-for-transparency-in-automated-decision-making ; issues paper https://www.oaic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0027/263925/ADM-Issues-Paper.pdf . The White & Case alert used in wave 1 returned HTTP 403 and is not needed.
findings.action: Put a dated board item now with a named owner. Decide and write down the honest position: if a clinician approves every note, Scribe plausibly is not making an ADM decision, but that argument has to be written, reviewed and reflected in the privacy policy before 10 December, not improvised in December. Separately source the turnover-threshold question rather than assuming it.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: Error analysis, not eval infrastructure, is where LLM work should go — but the 60-80% figure is two practitioners' self-report
findings.claim: The most-cited practitioner source on production evals reports that its authors spend 60-80% of their own development time on error analysis and evaluation rather than on automated checks, and states that "error analysis is the most important activity in evals". That is experienced-practitioner opinion, not a measurement of teams, and wave 1 rendered it as an industry statistic at high confidence. The protocol it gives is verified verbatim: annotate at least 30 traces personally, work up to a pool of roughly 100 diverse traces, continue to saturation, prefer binary labels over Likert because binary forces clearer thinking and more consistent labelling, validate any LLM judge on TPR/TNR against a held-out human-labelled set, and favour deterministic assertions over LLM judges in CI while running expensive judges asynchronously on production traffic. A team that is slow to ship LLM features and arguing about comment clarity in PRs is more likely failing on this axis than on code quality — that last sentence is inference, not evidence.
findings.evidence: Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, AI Evals FAQ, published 2025-05-28, modified 2026-09-01 — https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/ . Verifier checked each quoted specific against the page; the headline sentence reads first person: "we've spent 60-80% of our development time on error analysis and evaluation".
findings.action: Replace one sit-down PR review per week with a sit-down trace review: the team reads 30 real de-identified Scribe outputs together and writes failure labels. Same social mechanism Jason already has running, pointed at the thing that determines whether the product is good. Present the 60-80% number as an anecdote if it is quoted at all.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q4 tools

findings.title: One open eval asset exists for this product category; the second is a closed vendor leaderboard
findings.claim: Omi-Health's medical-note-eval is MIT-licensed and reusable: 300 synthetic doctor-patient dialogues with sentence-level IDs, 2,400 generated notes across 8 models, scored on prose quality, hallucinations, left-out safety facts (missed medications, allergies, assessments, plans) and cost/speed, using a 4-verifier LLM panel drawn from four model families with cross-family majority required. Being synthetic it is PHI-free, which is what makes it shareable across a firewalled team, CI and a vendor conversation. Two caveats wave 1 omitted: it is published by a commercial scribe vendor benchmarking the models its own product competes on, and its LLM panel has no reported agreement against human labels, so adopting its verdicts wholesale would violate the TPR/TNR rule from the finding above. vals.ai's MedScribe is not a second open asset — it is a closed vendor leaderboard produced in collaboration with Protege, with no expert-authorship or public-dataset claim — useful as a model-selection input only.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/Omi-Health/medical-note-eval — MIT, "Use the corpus, the scripts, and the methodology however you like"; "300 synthetic doctor-patient dialogues"; 2,400 notes / 8 models; metric "Left-out safety facts — missed medications, allergies, assessments, or plans"; "4-verifier LLM panel from 4 different families (Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Google); cross-family majority required". https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/medscribe — "Updated 9/3/2026", 100 rubrics, 22 models, Claude Opus 5 at 90.99%, with a stated caveat that accuracy tends to improve as outputs get longer. Both fetched 2026-09-05.
findings.action: Fork medical-note-eval and run it against Scribe's current prompt as a one-afternoon baseline, then TPR/TNR-check its panel against a small hand-labelled Scribe sample before trusting its scores. Adopt its four metric axes as the team's vocabulary. Use MedScribe as a model-selection input, not as a benchmark to reproduce, and note the length confound before optimising toward it.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q4 tools

findings.title: Kaiser Permanente published the in-product QA loop worth copying
findings.claim: The strongest named-team template for evaluating an ambient scribe in production is Kaiser Permanente's: a 10-week pilot in early 2024 across 63,000 encounters and more than 1,000 physicians before the 8-region rollout, running three parallel instruments — a 5-star rating on the draft note captured in-flow (14% of encounters rated: 47% five-star, 31% four-star, 7% one or two star), a modified Physician Documentation Quality Instrument scoring accuracy, thoroughness and perceived bias (4.35/5 from 1,252 responses), and structured coding of free-text comments (two QA staff read more than 3,600). The review panel was physicians, administrators, informaticists, safety officers, quality risk leaders and evaluators, not just engineers. The full deployment reportedly reached 7,260 physicians and about 2.5M encounters over Oct 2023 to Dec 2024 with 15,791 documentation hours saved; those NEJM Catalyst figures were not independently opened during verification.
findings.evidence: Permanente Medicine quality-assurance writeup, page dated 26 March 2025 — every figure verified verbatim by the verifier, including "Of the 14% of patient encounters that received ratings, 47% of ratings were 5-star, 31% were 4-star, and 7% received 1 or 2 stars", "1,252 responses to the PDQI questionnaire", average 4.35/5, and "Two quality team members read through more than 3,600 clinician free-text comments" — https://permanente.org/quality-assurance-informs-large-scale-use-of-ambient-ai-clinical-documentation/ . NEJM Catalyst, "Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes: Learnings after 1 Year and over 2.5 Million Uses" — https://catalyst.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/CAT.25.0040 (not opened during verification).
findings.action: Ship the in-note rating widget before the next model change. It is the cheapest regression detector Scribe can have, it doubles as the sampling frame for the trace reviews above, and the PDQI is an off-the-shelf validated rubric so nobody invents scoring criteria in a meeting. Given the TGA's post-market-monitoring finding, it is also the compliance artefact.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: The Effect service seam is the right place to make LLM work testable — but @effect/ai is self-described alpha
findings.claim: Modelling the LLM call as an Effect service is the correct seam and Effect documents it explicitly: mock, simulate or snapshot responses by providing an alternative implementation, and write business logic once with the provider deferred until runtime. The wave 1 form omitted that the same page says "The Effect AI integration packages are currently in the experimental / alpha stage", which matters when the recommendation is aimed at a regulated product whose framework is simultaneously mid-major-migration. So adopt the pattern — a Layer with a test implementation, which plain Effect gives today — rather than betting the Bedrock integration on that package. 14.ai is a real production reference for this shape in an AI-native support product (Effect schemas at every boundary, DI used to mock LLM providers and simulate failures without real API calls, token-stream duplication so one stream serves the user while a parallel one feeds storage and analytics, multi-provider fallback with stateful retry), but the public record is a third-party summary of a conference talk, not the team's own engineering write-up. It independently reports a steep initial learning curve and DI complexity at scale as costs.
findings.evidence: https://effect.website/docs/ai/introduction/ (re-fetched by the reconciler 2026-09-05): "mock, simulate, or snapshot responses just by providing an alternative implementation"; "Write your business logic once, and defer choosing the underlying provider ... until runtime"; and "The Effect AI integration packages are currently in the experimental / alpha stage." 14.ai patterns via ZenML's curated summary of a talk by 14.ai's co-founder — https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-reliable-ai-agent-systems-with-effect-typescript-framework . AWS surface: https://github.com/floydspace/effect-aws (60+ Effect-wrapped AWS clients, MIT).
findings.action: If Scribe's Bedrock call is not already a Layer with a test implementation, that is the highest-leverage refactor available: it turns "we can't test the AI bit" into ordinary tests and is the same seam that makes the au. residency control enforceable. Build it on plain Effect Layers, not on @effect/ai, while that package is alpha. Copy 14.ai's stream duplication to capture production traces for error analysis without touching the user path.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q4 tools

findings.title: Effect v4 is a budgetable spike, not a moving target — and the AWS client is the real gate
findings.claim: Effect v4 reached Release Candidate on 12 August 2026, and as of today `effect` still ships v3 on the `latest` dist-tag (3.22.1, published 2026-07-30) with v4 only on `rc` (4.0.0-rc.112, 2026-08-25). The migration is real — one shared version across packages, packages merged into core, an effect/unstable/* namespace with weaker semver guarantees, Effect.Do/bind/let removed in favour of Effect.gen, Cause flattened, the Tag static-accessor proxy gone, and Schema renames as the worst of it — though that breaking-change list is currently only reachable through a Mintlify-hosted mirror of the effect-smol docs, not the official site. Wave 1 dropped the vendor's own commitment in the same recap it cited: no broad breaking changes are planned for the RC cycle, and any that land will be narrow, communicated and carry a migration path. So this is a schedulable spike, not a shifting target. The binding constraint is dependency-side and more nuanced than the verifier's form: @effect-aws/client-bedrock-runtime's stable line (1.11.3, latest, published 2026-07-18) pins effect ">=3.0.4 <4.0.0", excluding v4 outright; a v4-targeting line exists only as a beta (2.0.0-beta.6, same day, peer range ">=4.0.0-beta.66 <5.0.0"). Adopting Effect v4 means running a beta AWS client.
findings.evidence: npm registry, queried by the reconciler 2026-09-05: `effect` dist-tags latest=3.22.1 (2026-07-30), rc=4.0.0-rc.112 (2026-08-25), beta=4.0.0-beta.107; @effect-aws/client-bedrock-runtime dist-tags latest=1.11.3 with peerDependencies {"effect": ">=3.0.4 <4.0.0"} and beta=2.0.0-beta.6 with {"effect": ">=4.0.0-beta.66 <5.0.0"}, both published 2026-07-18. RC date and the no-broad-breaking-changes commitment: https://effect.website/blog/effect-v4-rc-august-recap (page dated 31 August 2026; the RC announcement itself is at https://effect.website/blog/releases/effect/40-rc). Breaking-change list via the third-party mirror mintlify.wiki (the mintlify.com/effect-TS URL 308-redirects there). Practitioner migration, 2026-02-25, bundle 9,752 to 9,024 KiB and startup 589ms to 471ms — https://www.sandromaglione.com/newsletter/my-effect-v4-beta-migrations .
findings.action: Pin the Effect version explicitly and put a v4 spike on the roadmap with a named owner and a date, sized against the Schema surface. Make the AWS-client beta the go/no-go: the spike's first question is whether the team is willing to run @effect-aws 2.0.0-beta in production, or to call Bedrock through the plain AWS SDK behind its own Layer instead. Do not let this land in the same quarter as 10 December.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: The 'Effect is unshareable' diagnosis is one commenter's opinion; the remedy is worth doing anyway
findings.claim: The widely repeated complaint that Effect is unshareable — docs inadequate without a functional-programming background, three years of API churn making older articles obsolete, and community knowledge trapped in a Discord where search is near-useless — traces in this evidence base to a single Hacker News comment by one user in June 2024, in a thread of roughly eight or nine comments, and is two Effect major-version cycles stale. The 2026 bus-factor framing comes from an SEO content site and is opinion. The one independent production data point, 14.ai, reports a steep initial learning curve and dependency-injection complexity at scale. So the shape Jason described — the team resisting a pattern it has no shared vocabulary for, as with the barrel-file argument — is a plausible reading rather than a documented pattern, and the remedy stands on its own merits regardless.
findings.evidence: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40683256 (2024-06-14): all three quotes come from one comment by user srhtftw. Bus-factor framing (opinion): https://www.buildmvpfast.com/blog/effect-ts-functional-programming-typescript-production-2026 . Independent corroboration of costs: https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-reliable-ai-agent-systems-with-effect-typescript-framework .
findings.action: Write a one-page "the Effect we use" naming the roughly ten constructs in-bounds for this codebase (Effect.gen, Layer, Service, Schema, Stream, tagged errors) and explicitly parking the rest (Fibers, custom Schedules, STM) until someone justifies one in review. Ship it as a repo rule the work Claude Code reads too. Present it as a team decision, not as a fix for a documented industry problem.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q3 operator gaps

findings.title: The barrel-file numbers do not say what wave 1 said — but the dispute is still settleable by measurement
findings.claim: Vercel measured that importing from third-party barrel-file packages costs 200 to 800ms per package under the Next.js compiler, with @material-ui/icons at 10.2s across 11,738 modules. The post's conclusion is the opposite of the one wave 1 drew: it ships optimizePackageImports to remove that cost automatically, "making barrel files viable without sacrificing speed". The measurements concern node_modules packages under Next.js, not a team's own internal barrel files, which is what the two engineers were arguing about, and the "up to 40% faster cold starts" figure is explicitly attributed to Next.js 13.5 as a whole. So the claim that the objecting engineers were closer to the published evidence than the pattern is not supported, and neither the 28% nor the 40% figure transfers to an Effect/Lambda service without measurement. What survives is the generalisable point, and it is the useful one: this class of dispute has a five-minute local benchmark, so the review culture's fix is to measure cold start and bundle size both ways on the disputed PR and let the number decide, rather than arguing from taste, from provenance, or from a blog about a different toolchain.
findings.evidence: Vercel engineering blog, "How we optimized package imports in Next.js", 2023-10-13: "For many popular React packages, it takes 200~800ms just to import them"; "@material-ui/icons: 10.2s (11738 modules) -> 2.9s (632 modules)"; "next build runs ~28% faster"; "We've measured up to 40% faster cold starts" paired with other Next.js 13.5 improvements; and the stated conclusion that optimizePackageImports makes barrel files viable — https://vercel.com/blog/how-we-optimized-package-imports-in-next-js . Codified as an agent rule: https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/react-best-practices/rules/bundle-barrel-imports.md .
findings.action: Use the disputed PR as the worked example in the sit-down review experiment, but run the benchmark rather than citing the Vercel post: measure this repo's cold start and bundle size both ways in front of everyone. The norm being installed is "what does this cost", not "is this how we write code" — and it works only if the measurement is local, since the published numbers are about a different toolchain.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q3 operator gaps

findings.title: OpenTelemetry will not resolve the PHI-versus-error-analysis tension, and content capture is one opt-in away
findings.claim: OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions remain in Development status as of mid-2026, with every gen_ai.* attribute, span, metric and event carrying the Development badge; the attributes were deprecated in the core semconv repo and moved to open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai at v1.42.0 on 12 June 2026. Instrumenting to them is a moving target. No prompt content or tool arguments are captured by default because they can contain sensitive data — and enabling content capture is an explicit opt-in that then records full prompt messages, system prompts, tool schemas, tool arguments and tool results, which is exactly the switch a team doing error analysis will be tempted to flip. That default is right for PHI and wrong for the error-analysis practice above. Nobody's default resolves it: content traces need their own PHI-boundary store with the access control and audit logging of the clinical record, sampled deliberately, with the metadata layer the only thing that crosses out of it, and never shipped to a third-party eval SaaS without an equivalent residency and BAA position.
findings.evidence: https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/genai-observability/ : "By default, no prompt content or tool arguments are captured with GenAI telemetry, as these can contain sensitive data", and content capture "populates span attributes with full prompt messages, system prompts, tool schemas, tool arguments, and tool results". Development status corroborated by https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions (page dated 2026-05-21 despite the slug). The repo-split fact is true but is carried by neither cited page — its source is the semantic-conventions v1.42.0 release notes, 12 June 2026. Contrast posture from an AU vendor: audio deleted after draft generation, AU-only storage, no training on customer data — https://www.lyrebirdhealth.com/au/privacy .
findings.action: Decide and write down where Scribe's content traces live and who may read them, before choosing an eval or observability vendor, because that answer determines which vendors are eligible. Treat gen_ai.* metadata as the only thing that leaves the boundary, and make the content-capture opt-in a reviewed decision rather than a config flag someone flips during a debugging session.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: The 'time saved' business case for scribes rests on leader testimony, not measurement
findings.claim: PHTI's AI Taskforce, synthesising interviews and convenings with eight named US health systems (CommonSpirit, Intermountain, Mass General Brigham, MultiCare, Ochsner, Providence, UC San Diego, Yale New Haven) and published 25 March 2025, reports that ambient scribes are potentially effective at reducing clinician documentation time and cognitive load, while "health system leaders indicate that there are gaps in evidence regarding the impact of ambient scribes on productivity and financial performance". This is qualitative leader testimony, not a controlled study, and it is a 2025 source, not 2026. Two specifics wave 1 attached to it do not appear at that URL and need their own source: the roughly $600m invested in three years, and the heavy/partial/stopped three-cohort adoption pattern. The practical read stands: an outcome metric of minutes saved per consult claims something the published evidence does not yet support.
findings.evidence: Peterson Health Technology Institute, "Leading Health Systems: AI-Powered Scribes Alleviate Clinician Burnout; Financial Impact Unclear", 2025-03-25 — https://phti.org/announcement/ai-scribes-reduce-clinician-burnout/ ; coverage https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/ai-scribes-provider-burnout-financial-impact-peterson-health-technology-institute/743517/ .
findings.action: If the team's outcome metric is minutes saved per consult, swap it for sustained weekly active clinicians plus the drop-off cohort — measures the team can actually observe and defend. Source the cohort pattern separately if it is quoted, since the PHTI page does not carry it.
findings.question: Q2 team

findings.title: The recommended Effect Bedrock package cannot reach the only in-region path
findings.claim: The two AWS recommendations in this lane are mutually exclusive as written. @effect/ai-amazon-bedrock implements LanguageModel via Amazon Bedrock's Converse API, and the Sonnet 5 model card shows Converse as supported on bedrock-runtime and not-supported on bedrock-mantle — mantle accepts only the Messages API for this model. bedrock-mantle is the sole In-Region option (Melbourne, ap-southeast-4). So a team that follows the residency advice to its strictest conclusion cannot use the Effect Bedrock package to do it, and a team that adopts the package is committed to geo or global routing on bedrock-runtime. Both sources were open in wave 1 and the conflict was not noticed.
findings.evidence: Verified by the reconciler 2026-09-05. https://effect.website/docs/ai/introduction/ names @effect/ai-amazon-bedrock and states it supports "LanguageModel (via Amazon Bedrock's Converse API)". https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-anthropic-claude-sonnet-5.html : APIs supported on bedrock-mantle show Messages supported, Converse and Invoke not-supported; APIs on bedrock-runtime show Messages, Converse and Invoke supported; bedrock-mantle In-Region regions are us-east-1, us-gov-west-1, eu-north-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-4.
findings.action: Settle the routing decision before the client decision, not after. If au. geo on bedrock-runtime is the accepted position, the Effect package is available and the CI prefix check is the control. If In-Region Melbourne is required, plan on the Messages API through a plain client behind an Effect Layer and accept losing Guardrails, Knowledge base, Model evaluation, Agents and Flows with it.
findings.question: Q2 team, Q4 tools

findings.title: Cleveland Clinic published the enterprise rollout blueprint the QA finding does not cover
findings.claim: A peer-reviewed, in-period named-team case exists for deploying an ambient scribe at enterprise scale, and it answers the shipping-fast-and-safely half of the question that Kaiser's QA instrumentation does not. Cleveland Clinic describes a vendor-health-system deployment partnership built on four pillars — governance, training and onboarding, support, and real-time learning — which onboarded more than 4,000 ambulatory care clinicians in four months, published as a blueprint for other systems facing rapid enterprise-wide deployment. A companion 2026 paper treats ambient scribes as emerging infrastructure in the learning health system, covering governance across clinicians, patients, leaders, vendors and regulators.
findings.evidence: Verified by the reconciler 2026-09-05 via Crossref. "Accelerating ambient AI scribe enterprise-scale deployment: Cleveland Clinic's novel approach to health system-industry partnership", npj Health Systems, published 2026-08-11, doi 10.1038/s44401-026-00144-6; abstract: "four pillars: governance, training and onboarding, support, and real time learning. This partnership enabled deployment and onboarding of over 4000 ambulatory care clinicians in 4 months". Companion: "Ambient AI Scribes as Emerging Infrastructure in the Learning Health System", Learning Health Systems, published 2026-08-10, doi 10.1002/lrh2.70115. The nature.com full text is behind an IDP redirect and was not opened; the pilot-start date of 10 March 2025 asserted in the verifier's note is unverified.
findings.action: Read the npj paper before designing Scribe's rollout, and lift its four pillars as the rollout's section headings so the team is arguing about a published structure rather than inventing one. Do not quote figures beyond the abstract until the full text is obtained.
findings.question: Q2 team
